stemMd:
**Dara:** The city's requirement that restaurants post a letter grade for kitchen hygiene has not improved hygiene. In the year before the requirement took effect, 61 percent of inspected kitchens received the top grade; in the year after, 63 percent did.

**Milo:** Those figures are consistent with a large improvement. Inspectors tightened the criteria for the top grade at the moment the requirement took effect, so that many kitchens that would have earned the top grade under the old criteria fall short of the new one.

Dara and Milo are committed to disagreeing with each other about whether

options.label: A
options.textMd: kitchen hygiene in the city has improved since the posting requirement took effect

options.label: B
options.textMd: the city should repeal the requirement that restaurants post a letter grade

options.label: C
options.textMd: posting letter grades gives restaurants an incentive to improve kitchen hygiene

options.label: D
options.textMd: more than 63 percent of the kitchens inspected in the year after the requirement took effect would have received the top grade under the criteria used in the year before

options.label: E
options.textMd: the change in the percentage of inspected kitchens receiving the top grade shows that hygiene has not improved

explanationMd:
A point-at-issue question has a two-part test, and a choice must pass both: **each** speaker must be committed to a view about the statement, and their views must be **opposed**. Most wrong answers fail the first part, not the second.

Sort the two speakers first.

- **Dara** asserts a conclusion (hygiene has not improved) and offers one piece of evidence for it: the top-grade share moved only from 61 percent to 63 percent. Treating that movement as showing no improvement is not an aside — it is the whole of her argument, so she is committed to it.
- **Milo** does not assert that hygiene improved. His words are that the figures "are consistent with a large improvement", and he explains why: the bar for the top grade was raised at the same moment, so a steady 61-to-63 percent conceals kitchens that got better. He is denying the evidential force of Dara's statistic.

So the one statement they are both committed to and take opposite views on is that Dara's figures show hygiene has not improved. Dara affirms it, Milo denies it. That is choice (E).

How to check: write each speaker's position on the statement in one word — "yes", "no", or "silent" — and reject any choice that contains a "silent". On (A) Milo is silent, because saying data are consistent with improvement is not saying improvement occurred; on (D) Dara is silent, because she never discusses how kitchens would have been graded under other criteria. The pattern to remember is that a speaker who attacks an argument's *evidence* has not thereby denied its *conclusion*, and the conclusion is nearly always offered as a tempting wrong answer.

distractorRationale.a: Milo never claims that hygiene improved. He says only that Dara's figures are consistent with a large improvement, which leaves open that hygiene stayed flat. Because he takes no position on the conclusion itself, this is a statement Dara denies and Milo declines to affirm, which is not a disagreement.
distractorRationale.b: Neither speaker says anything about whether the requirement should be kept or repealed. The exchange is entirely about what the grading figures do and do not establish, so this choice introduces a policy question on which both are silent.
distractorRationale.c: Incentives are never mentioned by either speaker. Dara argues that the posted grades did not improve hygiene and Milo argues that her data cannot show that, and neither offers any account of why posting grades might or might not motivate restaurants.
distractorRationale.d: Milo is indeed committed to this: if many kitchens that would have earned the top grade under the old criteria now fall short, then under the old criteria the share would exceed the 63 percent actually recorded. But Dara says nothing about counterfactual grading under other criteria, so this is a claim one speaker makes and the other never addresses.

accessibilityText: A short two-speaker exchange. Dara says the city's restaurant hygiene letter-grade posting requirement has not improved hygiene, citing that 61 percent of inspected kitchens received the top grade in the year before the requirement and 63 percent in the year after. Milo replies that those figures are consistent with a large improvement, because inspectors tightened the criteria for the top grade when the requirement began, so many kitchens that would have earned the top grade under the old criteria fall short of the new one. The question asks what Dara and Milo are committed to disagreeing about. Five answer choices labelled A through E.

independentSolve.workingNotes: Dara treats 61%-to-63% as showing no improvement; Milo says 'Those figures are consistent with a large improvement', i.e. they do not show what Dara takes them to show. Both are committed on (e). (a) fails because Milo asserts only consistency with improvement, never that hygiene improved. See concern re (d).

review.notes: Each choice was scored as yes/no/silent for both speakers. Only (E) yields an affirm-deny pair. (A) fails because Milo asserts consistency with improvement rather than improvement; (D) fails because Dara never addresses counterfactual grading. Milo's wording was chosen deliberately so that he does not assert the conclusion, which keeps (A) undefensible. Awaiting blind independent solve.

quarantine.reason: The independent solver agreed with the key but found a SECOND defensible answer, so the item is ambiguous regardless of which answer was intended. Reviewer answered (e) and matched the key, but showed option (d) is also defensible: Milo explicitly commits to (d), and Dara is arguably committed to denying it, so a strong candidate can argue both. Needs a rewrite that closes the second reading.
